unit.title: Copywriting
unit.description: AIDA, PAS, features and benefits, headlines, microcopy, objections, curiosity, specificity, voice of customer words

cards.definition: A feature is what the product has, an advantage what it does, a benefit what the customer gains. Copy that sells leads with the benefit and proves it with the feature.
cards.example: Feature: 5,000 mAh battery. Advantage: lasts two days. Benefit: no more searching for a socket at 6 pm.

cards.definition: Precise claims beat vague ones: numbers, names, timeframes and concrete details make copy believable.
cards.example: Cut your reporting time from 4 hours to 20 minutes beats Save a lot of time.

cards.definition: The best copy reuses the exact words customers use in interviews, reviews and support tickets, not the jargon of the company.
cards.example: Customers say I never know what to cook tonight; the page headline becomes No more what do we eat tonight.

cards.definition: Good copy speaks to a single, precise person with one main idea and one call to action per piece.
cards.example: An email to restaurant owners about one problem (empty tables on Tuesday) with one button.

exercises.explain: A classic structure from the advertising of the early 20th century, still used for pages, emails and videos.

exercises.prompt: PAS is a copywriting framework. What does it stand for?
exercises.explain: Name the pain, make it felt, then offer the way out. Use it with care: agitation must stay honest.

exercises.prompt: Which line is a benefit rather than a feature?
choices: Leave work on time every evening
Automated reports in PDF and Excel
exercises.explain: Benefits describe the result in the life of the customer. Features are proof that come after.

choices: How a 12-room hotel filled 30 percent more rooms in winter
Boost your hotel business with our solution
The best tool for hotels on the market
exercises.explain: Numbers, a precise target and a timeframe make the claim concrete and believable.

exercises.prompt: A button says Submit. Which microcopy usually works better?
exercises.explain: Buttons that state what the user gets reduce doubt. Microcopy is small text with a big impact on conversion.

exercises.prompt: Where should you look for the words of your next landing page?
choices: Customer interviews, reviews and support tickets
The internal glossary of the product team
The homepage of the market leader
A list of trendy marketing buzzwords
exercises.explain: Voice of customer copy: when visitors read their own words, they feel understood.

exercises.prompt: A curiosity gap headline is fine even if the article never delivers on its promise.
exercises.explain: False. That is clickbait: it may win the click but loses trust, raises bounce and hurts the brand. Curiosity must be paid back.

exercises.prompt: Your offer is expensive and visitors hesitate. Which block do you add near the call to action?
choices: Answers to objections: price, risk, results, time
A longer history of the company since 1998
A list of every feature of the product
Links to the social profiles of the brand
exercises.explain: Objection handling removes the last doubts: guarantee, ROI, testimonials, what happens after the purchase.

exercises.prompt: In the inverted pyramid style, where does the most important information go?
exercises.explain: Readers skim. Lead with the key point, then details. It also helps search engines and AI answers quote you.

exercises.prompt: Put a PAS email in order.
steps: Subject line naming the pain: Empty tables on Tuesday?
Problem: quiet weekdays cost you 2,000 euros a month
Agitate: staff paid, food wasted, rent due anyway
Solution: a midweek offer sent to your past diners
Call to action: Try it free for 14 days
exercises.explain: Problem, agitation, solution, then one clear action. The subject line already speaks to the problem.
